t: Find Target Indices After Sorting Array — Sort-and-Scan vs. Pure Counting
o: **Understanding the problem.** After sorting `nums` in non-decreasing order we must list every index holding `target`, in increasing order. Sorting makes all copies of the target adjacent, so the answer is always one contiguous block of indices: `[1,2,5,2,3]` sorted is `[1,2,2,3,5]`, so `target = 2` occupies indices 1 and 2, while `target = 3` and `target = 5` occupy the single indices 3 and 4. If the target never appears, the block is empty. Constraints are tiny (`n <= 100`, values `<= 100`), so an $O(n \log n)$ sort-and-scan passes easily — but they also hint at an $O(n)$ alternative: only *how many* elements are below the target and how many equal it actually matter.
k: After sorting, every occurrence of target sits in one contiguous block, so the answer indices are consecutive.
The block starts exactly at the number of elements strictly smaller than target — counting beats sorting.
Duplicates are interchangeable once sorted, so the original arrangement never matters.

a.i: The literal reading of the statement: sort, then walk once collecting matches. Sorting clusters equal values, so the matching indices emerge already sorted.
a.t: O(n log n) — the sort dominates; the scan is linear.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary beyond the output (in-place sort).

a.n: Approach 2: Count Below and Equal (No Sort)
a.i: We never need the sorted array itself, only where the target block starts and how long it is. All values < target precede it in sorted order, so the first target index equals `less`, and `cnt` occurrences give the block length.
s: Count less = elements strictly smaller than target, cnt = elements equal to target.
If cnt == 0 return an empty list.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with two counters.

w: Propose Approach 1 first, then offer Approach 2 as the no-sort upgrade — it signals that you noticed only counts matter. Pitfalls: JavaScript needs a numeric comparator `(a, b) => a - b` because the default sort is lexicographic; both approaches handle the empty case naturally (empty range / zero matches). Follow-ups: return the indices the target held before sorting (sort value-index pairs), or answer many targets against one array with prefix counts.
